I think the strongest version of my question is this. Take a mathematician who is not working on foundations and is mostly focussed on formal verification of mathematical theorems such as Fermat's Last Theorem or the Navier-Stokes problem. Say they were handed a theorem prover which had Nat and Nat.rec axiomatised, and which then implemented Lean's type theory but without inductive types other than structures (I am not 100% sure that this makes sense -- I mean no inductive keyword but a structure keyword, i.e. "only allow inductive types which can be created with structure"). Do they have enough machinery to build proofs of these hard theorems?

I'm sure that from an efficiency point of view we would be losing a lot. But I am just talking about a theoretical question here. I know very little about the kernel but I know that a lot of fuss is being made about nested inductive types being on perhaps shaky foundational ground (I am just looking at https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3808322 for example), and I'm aware of the recent discussion about nested inductives after the soundness bug issues.

Am I right in thinking that Lean doesn't "need" nested inductives, because they can be simulated using inductives? Obviously mathematicians need Nat and they certainly need structures, but do mathematicians even need general inductive types? I see List occasionally in mathlib but this is just a sigma type of Fin n -> alpha, and both Fin and Sigma are structures. I am not sure I've ever seen a nested inductive type in Mathlib. I understand that nested inductives are there for convenience when programming but I am wondering what the role of inductives is in mathematics beyond Nat.
How can you state Or without inductive? I don't see how it can be done with only structure.

I think the strongest version of my question is this. Take a mathematician who is not working on foundations and is mostly focussed on formal verification of mathematical theorems such as Fermat's Last Theorem or the Navier-Stokes problem. Say they were handed a theorem prover which had Nat and Nat.rec axiomatised, and which then implemented Lean's type theory but without inductive types other than structures (I am not 100% sure that this makes sense -- I mean no inductive keyword but a structure keyword, i.e. "only allow inductive types which can be created with structure"). Do they have enough machinery to build proofs of these hard theorems?

As Joachim's https://github.com/nomeata/lean-inductive-models showed we can construct inductive types from just Eq Nat PUnit PSigma' Quot in principle. You do loose definitional equalties when you would use these constructions in vanilla Lean but the type theory can in principle be designed in a way where you can extend definitional equality with provable equalities and recover all the behavior you are interested in.

Note that these kinds of constructions are completely standard in HOL systems. For example all of HOL Light's axioms can be found on its Wikipedia page and it manages to build up inductive types regardless (although HOL is of course a non-dependent logic)

Am I right in thinking that Lean doesn't "need" nested inductives, because they can be simulated using inductives?

Yes, that is in fact what the kernel does internally to implement them.

I understand that nested inductives are there for convenience when programming but I am wondering what the role of inductives is in mathematics beyond Nat.

Fortunately questions like these are easy to ask in Lean:

import Lean
import Mathlib

namespace Lean
namespace CollectInductives

structure State where
  visited : NameSet := {}
  inducts : NameSet := {}

abbrev M := StateRefT State CoreM

partial def collect (declName : Name) : M Unit := do
  if (← get).visited.contains declName then return
  modify fun s => { s with visited := s.visited.insert declName }
  let some info := (← getEnv).find? declName | return
  match info with
  | .inductInfo _ => modify fun s => { s with inducts := s.inducts.insert declName }
  | .ctorInfo v   => modify fun s => { s with inducts := s.inducts.insert v.induct }
  | .recInfo v    => modify fun s => { s with inducts := v.all.foldl .insert s.inducts }
  | _             => pure ()
  for c in info.getUsedConstantsAsSet do
    collect c

end CollectInductives

def collectInductives (declName : Name) : CoreM (Array Name) := do
  let (_, s) ← CollectInductives.collect declName |>.run {}
  return s.inducts.toArray

end Lean
open Lean Elab Command in
elab "#inductives_in " id:ident : command => do
  let declName ← liftCoreM <| realizeGlobalConstNoOverload id
  let inducts ← liftCoreM <| collectInductives declName
  let env ← getEnv
  let inducts := inducts.filter (!isStructure env ·)
  logInfo m!"{inducts.size} inductive types:\n{inducts.toList}"

I think Gödel says you can encode everything as natural numbers, and then theoretically formalize all of math using Nat?

@Kevin Buzzard I'd argue that all the "generate something recursively from some initial data" constructions are naturally phrased as inductives (no suprise), and indeed you have docs#Filter.GenerateSets, docs#TopologicalSpace.GenerateOpen, docs#MeasurableSpace.GenerateMeasurable, ... that are all non-structure inductives in mathlib

As Joachim's https://github.com/nomeata/lean-inductive-models showed we can construct inductive types from just Eq Nat PUnit PSigma' Quot in principle.

It's not clear that @Joachim Breitner's translation is complete. And this matters for at least @Kevin Buzzard 's foundation question of whether they are "on shaky ground", at least in the default kernel which fully implements them. I think in theory there are a few cases the translation doesn't fully cover, where the translation code will fail. I have been using an LLM to explore more carefully when this is the case, and I'm still trying to understand, so forgive me if I say something wrong. I think some of those cases, and maybe all of them, can be extended to be more complete. But I'm not sure about Projections from Prop structures with data fields (mentioned in lean4#7637). My LLM suggests the translation fails for that, and it isn't as easy a fix (but might still be consistent nonetheless).

But to be clear, the translation does seem to cover much code used in practice (like Mathlib, FLT, and Navier-Stokes) since the translation and corresponding kernel (as in con-leche) were able to successfully check those.

Jason Rute said:

at least in the default kernel which fully implements them

This is a misunderstanding of Lean's kernel, which has always defined nested inductives via (partial) translation validation. inductive-models does complete that translation and so could potentially reject more inductives (ideally when they should be rejected).

@Sebastian Ullrich, I agree I'm likely misunderstanding. But what you just said seems to imply there may be cases where the Lean kernel partial translation validation is too partial and doesn't reject some nested inductives that ideally should be rejected. But inductive-models does do this. Is this correct, or am I misunderstanding? And if it is correct, that is at least in spirit what I'm trying to get at. The inductive-models approach and con-leche seem to be on more solid foundational footing, and it is not clear that a full lean kernel wouldn't accept a nested inductive that we wouldn't want it to accept (because it is unsound with respect to Mario's set theory model, or worse, inconsistent). Hopefully this isn't the case, but the existence of inductive models doesn't tell us this in general about the Lean kernel, only about specific projects it is used to check, right?

Jason Rute said:

The inductive-models approach and con-leche seem to be on more solid foundational footing

Yes, and I think this the relevant part for this thread. Use lake comparator --paranoid in 4.35+, which includes con-leche, and nested inductives are gone from the TCB fully.

Ok. I think we are agreed. One small point is that con-leche is great, but it has to be used in practice (say, via --paranoid) to be of value. This means using it for all AI math repos (including in Palomar, Tau Ceti, Lean Pool, Prove2Me, etc). Hopefully one day, we will also know nested inductives in Lean are also fine without con-leche (and it seems there is a path towards doing that: #AI authored projects > con-leche, a lean checker with a proof of consistency @ 💬 )
Nested inductive types show up well beyond “type theory” or foundations. A lot of PL semantics work that define even basic languages use nested inductives. In theoretical CS Trees are everywhere.
The title of the thread did specify "mathematicians".
Okay fair. I think a lot of TCS people do cross the boundary. Noga Alon comes to mind.

Henrik Böving said:

... easy :thinking:? Jokes aside, this is beautiful but perhaps if the mathematician whom Kevin had in mind gets conclvinced by this, they're confident enough to forge their own opinion on nested inductives.

My "eink0rn" kernel also, internally, does not have any notion of nested inductives, much like the lean-inductive-models; a lowering pass is used to remove them. (It also does a number of other lowering passes to add other extensions to the type theory.)

For people interested in this I've also been continuing work on my elaborator which can, among many other things, remove nested inductives in your own Lean code so that no comparator call is needed; it also adds a good chunk of other fancy stuff.
We worked on the subject, and we discuss how to implement them better in Lean with Mario and others at FLOC following our work published last year at PLDI https://inria.hal.science/hal-05366368
